claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in nanoscale FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers under sustained loading is controlled by a synergy between interface-mediated dislocation activity and diffusional creep.
Interfaces in these multilayers exhibit severe lattice distortion.
Interfaces in these multilayers exhibit spatial variations in short-range order.
The heterogeneous interfaces are preferential sites for stress-induced dislocation nucleation.
The heterogeneous interfaces promote dislocation climb.
The heterogeneous interfaces provide enhanced local atomic-diffusion pathways.
Compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and short-range-order variations create locally softer interface zones.
The simultaneous operation of dislocation-mediated plasticity and diffusional creep causes progressive accumulation of plastic strain.
The proposed deformation response differs from that of conventional, compositionally simpler metallic multilayers.
A nanoscale coating with alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy-alloy layers thinner than 100 nm can retain well-defined coherent interfaces despite its compositional complexity.
The proposed comparison subjects HEA and conventional multilayers of comparable dimensions to identical constant-stress creep conditions.
The proposed tests use temperatures of approximately 0.3–0.5 Tm, stresses on the order of 100 MPa, and durations of hundreds of hours.
The HEA multilayers will have a higher creep rate than conventional metallic multilayers with comparable nanoscale dimensions.
Sustained loading of the HEA multilayers will produce distinctive interfacial slip steps and evidence of localized diffusion and dislocation activity.
Deformation will evolve from a primarily dislocation-mediated regime to a mixed regime with significant diffusional creep.
Conventional nanoscale metallic multilayers such as Cu/Nb are typically governed by dislocation glide and standard diffusional creep without amplified effects from compositional heterogeneity.
The proposed mechanism applies to multilayers with layer thicknesses below approximately 100 nm at temperatures of approximately 0.3–0.5 Tm.
The mechanism may not apply to thicker layers, temperatures outside the creep regime, or compositions that do not produce sufficient lattice distortion and short-range order.
A failure to observe a higher creep rate and the predicted combined interfacial dislocation and diffusion signatures relative to the conventional control would reject the hypothesis.
